blueprint_topic: Management of Care — individualized discharge planning, home-safety barriers, caregiver support, and referral/resource coordination
stem: A client preparing for discharge after total knee replacement lives alone in a two-story home with loose rugs, no bathroom grab bars, and no available help for the first several days. Which nursing action is the priority?

options.A: Reassess discharge readiness with the team and arrange needed home modifications, support, or a safer temporary setting before discharge.
options.B: Provide written fall-prevention instructions and continue the planned discharge because the client can already ambulate with a walker.
options.C: Request additional stair training from physical therapy and base discharge mainly on stair performance rather than the home and support barriers.
options.D: Arrange a home-health visit after discharge and leave the identified environmental and caregiver gaps to be addressed during that first visit.

rationale: A is correct. Current AAOS OrthoInfo guidance for recovery after total knee replacement states that direct home discharge may be unsafe when the client lacks help at home or has another barrier to self-care; AAOS also recommends preparing the home by removing loose rugs, installing bathroom safety equipment, considering a temporary first-floor living space, and arranging help during early recovery. NCSBN places safe discharge, multidisciplinary collaboration, referral assessment, plan-of-care updates, and resource use within Management of Care. B is incorrect because written instructions do not resolve the identified environmental and support barriers. C is incorrect because stair training may be useful, but the discharge problem is broader than stair performance and includes the home environment and lack of assistance. D is incorrect because a later home-health visit does not make an unsafe discharge plan acceptable when barriers are already known before discharge.
educational_objective: Individualize postoperative discharge planning by identifying home and caregiver barriers, coordinating needed modifications or support, and changing the discharge plan when the home setting is not yet safe.
source_organization: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS); National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)

correction_summary: Original Q1872 had a strong correct-answer length cue (A 223 characters vs substantially shorter distractors) and cartoonish distractors that denied obvious home-safety relevance. Stem was narrowed to total knee replacement to align directly with current AAOS evidence, and all four options were rebuilt as realistic discharge-planning alternatives. A was then tightened after GitHub reread to eliminate the residual length cue while preserving the required interdisciplinary/home-safety action. Independent second-pass reread found no unresolved source, clinical, ambiguity, cueing, blueprint, or second-answer conflict.

option_audit.A: Correct; resolves known environmental/support barriers through team reassessment and concrete discharge-plan modification, consistent with AAOS and NCSBN.
option_audit.B: Plausible but insufficient; education is appropriate, yet it does not resolve the known home hazards and lack of support before discharge.
option_audit.C: Plausible PT-focused distractor; stair training may help but cannot substitute for addressing rugs, bathroom safety and lack of caregiver support.
option_audit.D: Plausible continuity-of-care distractor; home health may be useful, but knowingly deferring existing safety/support barriers until after discharge is not the best plan.
